passage:
Week 1: Sarita watched her sister Himani try to convince Dadi to pay the electricity bill on the phone instead of queuing at the office. "It's easy, Dadi, just press here!" Dadi folded her arms. "And if the money goes to the wrong place?" Himani pushed harder; Dadi stopped talking to her for a day.
Week 2: Sarita sat with Dadi over tea. "What worries you most?" "That I'll press the wrong thing, lose money, and not know how to fix it." Sarita nodded. "That's a real worry."
Week 4: They tried one small bill together, the water bill, with Dadi pressing every button herself and a paper receipt printed afterwards. Dadi held the receipt up to the light. "Next month, electricity," she said.

qa.q: Which bill did Sarita and Dadi try first?
qa.a: They tried the water bill first.

qa.q: What was Dadi worried about?
qa.a: Dadi worried she would press the wrong thing, lose money and not know how to fix it.

qa.q: Why did Sarita's approach work where Himani's didn't?
qa.a: Sarita asked about the fear, treated it as real, and tried one small bill with Dadi in control and a paper receipt, instead of pushing the whole change at once.

qa.q: How might Himani feel after Dadi stopped talking to her for a day?
qa.a: Himani probably felt hurt and frustrated, since she only meant to make things easier, and may learn from watching Sarita's slower way.

grounding: Shows a young woman noticing an elder resist a small change, respecting the fear behind it and trying a small pilot instead of pushing.

passage: Swati, you're frustrated that the senior staff won't use the new scheduling software? Let your Neelam aunty tell you about the bank in 1998, when I was twenty-four. We were moving from ledgers to computers. Mr. Pillai, who had kept the ledgers for thirty years, refused to touch the keyboard. The young officers laughed at him and complained to the manager. I watched him instead. His hands shook when he thought no one was looking. It wasn't stubbornness; he was afraid of looking foolish after thirty years of being the expert. So I asked if he'd try just one account on the computer, with me beside him, and keep his ledger too. Within a month, he was teaching the others shortcuts.

qa.q: How long had Mr. Pillai kept the ledgers?
qa.a: Mr. Pillai had kept the ledgers for thirty years.

qa.q: What was Mr. Pillai afraid of?
qa.a: He was afraid of looking foolish after thirty years of being the expert, which is why his hands shook when he thought no one was looking.

qa.q: What could Swati take from Neelam aunty's story?
qa.a: Swati could look for the fear behind the resistance and suggest a small, supported trial, like one schedule in the software while the old method stays, instead of complaining.

qa.q: How might the laughter of the young officers have affected Mr. Pillai?
qa.a: Their laughter likely confirmed his fear of looking foolish, making him hold on to the ledgers even more tightly.

grounding: Shows a young professional noticing an elder colleague's fear behind resisting change and using a small pilot rather than pushing.

passage: It was the Diwali rush at the family sweet shop in Indore, customers three deep at the counter, and half of them kept asking, "Do you take phone payment?" Gargi, home from her job in Pune, had suggested a QR code last year. Papa had refused: "Cash is honest. Phones break." This time, with no time to argue, she watched him turn away two customers and saw his jaw tighten each time. She didn't push. In a quiet minute she knelt by his stool. "What if the money doesn't come?" he said quietly. "That's the worry, na?" He nodded. "Just today, just for the big boxes," she offered, "and I'll show you each payment arriving on your phone." By closing time, Papa was checking his phone after every sale, pleased.

qa.q: How many customers did Papa turn away while Gargi watched?
qa.a: Papa turned away two customers.

qa.q: What was Papa really worried about?
qa.a: Papa worried that the money wouldn't actually arrive, and his earlier "Cash is honest" covered that fear.

qa.q: What made Gargi's offer work even in the Diwali rush?
qa.a: She kept it tiny, just today and just the big boxes, and showed each payment arriving, so the feared cost could be checked right away.

qa.q: How might Papa feel by closing time?
qa.a: Papa seems pleased and more confident, checking each payment himself, and perhaps a little proud of trying something new. 😊

grounding: Shows a young woman noticing her father's resistance to a small change, respecting the fear behind it and offering a tiny trial instead of pushing.

passage:
Wednesday night
Did something small today that felt big. Our office allows two work-from-home days, but I've come in all five days since I joined, just because that's how I started. On Sunday I asked myself: if I were new and there were no pattern yet, what would I pick? Honestly, two home days, to skip the ninety-minute bus ride. My fear was that Yogesh, my manager, would think I'm slacking. So I tested just one day: today. I shared my work by ten o'clock. He replied, "Thanks, looks good." That's it. No raised eyebrow. I finished early and called Mummy, who said her girl sounded less tired. Trying one more next week.
Swati

qa.q: How long is Swati's bus ride?
qa.a: Swati's bus ride is ninety minutes.

qa.q: What was Swati afraid would happen if she worked from home?
qa.a: She feared Yogesh would think she was slacking, which had kept her coming in all five days out of habit.

qa.q: Why was testing a single day a wise step?
qa.a: It checked the feared cost in a small, safe way; when Yogesh just said "looks good", Swati had real evidence instead of a guess.

qa.q: How might Yogesh see Swati's first home day?
qa.a: Yogesh seems to see nothing unusual, just good work on time, which suggests the fear lived more in Swati's head than in the manager's view.

grounding: Shows a young woman asking what she would choose if there were no default and testing one small change to see if the feared cost appears.

passage: Every year, the family's soybean crop in their village near Latur went to Seth Ramdas's shop, because that's where Dada had always sold. Sonali, twenty-five and back from her agriculture diploma, asked a simple question at dinner: "If we'd never heard of Ramdas, where would we sell?" Her brother Saurabh laughed. "Where else?" But she had seen the new farmers' collective in town posting higher rates on a board. The fear at the table was real: Ramdas might refuse them next year. So Sonali suggested a test. Just one trolley to the collective, the rest to Ramdas as usual. The collective paid better and on time. Ramdas, when he heard, only said, "Bring the rest."

qa.q: What did Sonali see the farmers' collective doing in town?
qa.a: She saw the collective posting higher rates on a board.

qa.q: What was the family afraid would happen if they sold elsewhere?
qa.a: They feared Ramdas might refuse to buy from them next year, after the family had always sold to him.

qa.q: Why was sending just one trolley a smart test?
qa.a: It let the family see whether the feared cost appeared while keeping most of the crop with Ramdas, so the risk stayed small.

qa.q: How might Saurabh see his sister's question now?
qa.a: Saurabh, who laughed at first, may now see the question as useful, since the test found a better option without harming the old one.

grounding: Shows a young woman asking which buyer the family would choose if none were the default and testing one small change to see if the feared cost appears.

passage: Ritu, you're sad because your teacher said you got three wrong? Let your Kalyani Nani tell you about your Mama when he was eight. One day he came home dancing. "Amma, I got eight out of ten in the spelling test!" He made me pin the paper on the wall. The next week, a different teacher returned the same kind of test and said, "Two wrong, be careful." He came home and cried under the table. Eight right, two wrong, both times! Same score. I showed him both papers side by side. He looked from one to the other for a long time, and then he said, "But the first one felt better." He still laughs about it.

qa.q: What did Mama score in both spelling tests?
qa.a: He got eight right and two wrong both times.

qa.q: Why did young Mama cry under the table the second week?
qa.a: The teacher said "two wrong", so he felt he had failed, even though it was the same score that made him dance the week before.

qa.q: What could Ritu try with the teacher's comment about three wrong?
qa.a: Ritu could say the score the other way round too, how many were right, and look at both before deciding how to feel.

qa.q: How might the teacher who said "Two wrong, be careful" feel on seeing him cry?
qa.a: That teacher might be surprised and sorry, since the words were meant to help him notice mistakes, not to make eight out of ten feel like failing.

grounding: Shows a boy happy when told he got eight of ten right and sad when told he got two wrong, though the facts were identical.

passage: Rain was flooding the school gate, and the teacher was rushing to send everyone home, so she gave the maths quiz results in a hurry. To one row she said, "You all got eight right, well done!" To Bhupen's row, the next one, she said, "Two wrong, check your carrying." Bhupen trudged home under Alka didi's umbrella, kicking puddles. "I'm bad at maths," he said. Alka didi had seen his paper. "You got eight right. Same as Rinku's row, and they were cheering." "But she said two wrong." "Two wrong is eight right." Bhupen stopped in a puddle and counted on his fingers. His face slowly brightened. "So I'm... good?"

qa.q: What did the teacher say to Bhupen's row?
qa.a: She said, "Two wrong, check your carrying."

qa.q: Why did Bhupen feel he was bad at maths?
qa.a: Hearing "two wrong" made him focus on the mistakes, so the same score that made another row cheer felt like failure to him.

qa.q: How could the teacher give results next time, even in a rush?
qa.a: She could say both parts, like "eight right, two to check", so every child hears the full picture and not just the mistakes.

qa.q: How might Rinku's row feel compared with Bhupen's?
qa.a: Rinku's row went home cheering with the same score, simply because they heard "eight right" instead of "two wrong".

grounding: Shows a boy feeling bad at maths when told he got two wrong, though another row cheered at hearing the same score as eight right.

passage: In their flat in Thane, Pradeep, nine, came back from football coaching and threw his bag on the sofa. "I'm the worst. Coach said I missed two penalties." His older cousin Chaitanya looked up from his laptop. "How many did you take?" "Ten." "So you scored eight?" Pradeep paused. "Yeah." "Eight out of ten is better than anyone in my college team." Pradeep sat down slowly. "Coach didn't say it like that." "Coach said the same thing, just the other way round." Pradeep grinned, then frowned. "Then why did I feel so bad?" Chaitanya shrugged. "Because you only heard the missing part."

qa.q: How many penalties did Pradeep take?
qa.a: Pradeep took ten penalties.

qa.q: Why does Pradeep feel he's the worst?
qa.a: Pradeep feels discouraged because Coach said he missed two, so he only heard the missing part, though the same result was eight goals out of ten.

qa.q: What could Pradeep do the next time coach gives feedback?
qa.a: He could ask himself what the result sounds like said the other way, goals scored as well as missed, before deciding how he feels.

qa.q: How might coach react on hearing that Pradeep felt like the worst?
qa.a: Coach would probably be surprised, having meant "missed two" as a small tip about ten mostly good penalties.

grounding: Shows a boy who feels terrible hearing he missed two penalties, then brightens when the same result is put as eight scored.

passage: In the school gym in Valencia, the basketball coach pinned up the shooting stats. Next to Alejandro's name: "Missed 40%." He read it and felt his chest drop. That evening he told Freya he was thinking of quitting the team. "Forty percent failure, Freya. That's almost half." Freya pulled up her own sheet on her phone. On the girls' team sheet, the coach had written each player's number the other way round: "Scored 60%." "Your number's the same as mine," she said. "I felt great about mine." Alejandro stared at the two sheets. "Sixty percent sounds... good, actually." He stopped talking about quitting.

qa.q: What did the sheet say next to Alejandro's name?
qa.a: The sheet said "Missed 40%."

qa.q: Why did Alejandro think of quitting the team?
qa.a: Seeing his result written as a 40 percent failure made it feel like almost half was bad, which dragged his mood down and nearly his choice with it.

qa.q: What habit could help Alejandro when he sees a percentage like this?
qa.a: He could rewrite it both ways, missed and scored, before reacting, so the wording doesn't make his decisions for him.

qa.q: How might Freya feel about having the same number and feeling great?
qa.a: Freya may be amused and a little surprised that the same result could make one friend proud and the other ready to quit.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy ready to quit over a result worded as 40 percent missed, until the same figure framed as 60 percent scored changes his mood.

passage: At the coaching institute, the mock-test results appeared on the corridor screen: "Dhruv: 40% incorrect." Dhruv went pale and walked straight past the canteen. In the counselling room, Sarita ma'am found him staring at the floor. "I'm failing, ma'am. Forty percent wrong." She turned her laptop toward him. "Look at your printed report card instead." It said: "Accuracy 60%. Batch average 52%." Dhruv read it twice. "That's the same test?" "Same test, same you." "Then why does the screen say it like that?" Sarita ma'am sighed. "Someone chose that wording. Your reaction came from the words, not from the score." Dhruv looked a little less pale.

qa.q: What was the batch average on the printed report card?
qa.a: The batch average was 52%.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv go pale and skip the canteen?
qa.a: Dhruv felt ashamed and worried because the screen framed his result as 40% incorrect, so it felt like failing. That wording, not the score itself, sank his mood.

qa.q: What could the institute change about how results are shown?
qa.a: It could show accuracy and the batch average together, or both correct and incorrect, so students don't react to one gloomy word.

qa.q: How might Sarita ma'am feel about the corridor screen?
qa.a: Sarita ma'am seems frustrated with the wording, since it made a student feel he was failing when his score was above average.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy crushed by a result worded as 40 percent incorrect until he sees the same score framed as 60 percent accuracy.

passage:

passage: Anirban, before you buy that "eighty percent success rate" course, let your Dolma aunty tell you something from when I was nineteen, a student in Darjeeling. A shop near the college had a sign on a winter jacket: "Twenty percent off! Save big!" The shop across the road sold the identical jacket with a sign that said, "You pay eighty percent of the price." Same price, I checked later. I felt I'd won something at the first shop, and I'd have walked straight past the second. And at the canteen, the "ninety percent fat-free" cake sold out every day, while nobody touched the one labelled "contains ten percent fat". Same cake, Anirban. The words did the choosing.

qa.q: What did the first shop's sign say?
qa.a: It said, "Twenty percent off! Save big!"

qa.q: Why did young Dolma feel she'd won something at the first shop?
qa.a: The "twenty percent off" wording made the price feel like a gain, while the same price described as paying eighty percent sounded like a loss.

qa.q: What could Anirban check before buying the "eighty percent success rate" course?
qa.a: Anirban could flip it to "twenty percent don't succeed", ask what that means in real numbers, and compare it with other courses before paying.

qa.q: How might the shop with the "you pay eighty percent" sign fare with the same jacket?
qa.a: That shop would likely sell far fewer jackets, even at the same price, simply because its wording made the deal sound like a loss.

grounding: Shows a student pulled toward offers worded as savings or percent fat-free and put off by the same figures worded as a cost.

passage: Madhav had ten minutes before the electronics shop closed, and his phone battery was at three percent. He needed a laptop for college, and the salesman, Shankar, was talking fast. "This warranty covers ninety percent of repair costs, sir. Peace of mind!" Madhav nodded; it sounded great. Then, at the billing counter, the cashier read from the form: "So you understand you'll pay ten percent of every repair yourself, plus the warranty fee?" Madhav hesitated. Suddenly it sounded like a trap. Same warranty, same fee. He stood there with his card half out, the shutters rattling down, trying to decide which sentence was the true one.

qa.q: What did the cashier say Madhav would pay?
qa.a: The cashier said he would pay ten percent of every repair himself, plus the warranty fee.

qa.q: Why did the warranty suddenly sound like a trap to Madhav?
qa.a: The cashier described the same deal as a cost he would pay, and that loss wording made it feel worse than the salesman's "covers ninety percent".

qa.q: How could Madhav judge the warranty on its own merits?
qa.a: He could write both versions side by side, work out the actual rupee cost of a typical repair, and ask for a day to decide rather than choosing in a rush.

qa.q: How might Shankar see the cashier's wording?
qa.a: Shankar may feel annoyed, since the gain-worded pitch was working and the cashier's version made the same deal sound like a loss.

grounding: Shows a student drawn in by a warranty worded as a gain and put off by the same terms worded as a loss, under time pressure.

passage: On the Delhi metro, Rashmi saw an ad for an evening coding course: "Register early and SAVE ₹2,000!" She smiled and took a photo. That night her friend Yash forwarded the same course's email: "A late fee of ₹2,000 applies after 1 June." Rashmi frowned. "Ugh, they're charging a penalty? That's so greedy." Yash laughed. "Rashmi, it's the same two thousand. Same course, same date." She looked at the photo and the email side by side. One made her feel clever; the other made her feel cheated. "Why do I like one and hate the other?" she asked. "Because ads know you better than you do," Yash said.

qa.q: What did the email say applies after 1 June?
qa.a: A late fee of ₹2,000 applies after 1 June.

qa.q: Why did the email make Rashmi feel cheated?
qa.a: The email framed the same two thousand as a penalty she would lose, while the ad framed it as savings she would gain, and losses feel worse.

qa.q: What could Rashmi do the next time an offer tugs at her?
qa.a: She could rewrite the offer the opposite way and in plain rupees, then decide whether the course is worth that price regardless of the wording.

qa.q: How might the course's advertisers see Rashmi's two reactions?
qa.a: The advertisers probably know that "save" attracts more people than "late fee", which is why the ad she saw first used the gain wording.

grounding: Shows a student attracted by an offer worded as savings and put off by the same amount worded as a late fee, as ads intend.

passage:
"Papa, the brochure says seventy percent of their students get into top colleges," said Gargi's younger brother, waving it.
"Seventy percent!" Yogesh said. "That's the school, then."
Gargi took the brochure. "Let's say it three ways. Seventy percent get in. Thirty percent don't. And in numbers: their batch last year was forty students, so twenty-eight got in and twelve didn't."
"Twelve didn't," Yogesh repeated slowly.
"The other school says sixty percent, but their batch was two hundred. That's a hundred and twenty students."
"So it depends how you say it."
"Exactly. I'm not saying which one. I just want us to see it straight before choosing."

qa.q: How many students were in the first school's batch last year?
qa.a: The first school's batch last year had forty students.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh repeat "Twelve didn't" slowly?
qa.a: Hearing the same result as a loss and in real numbers made it feel different from "seventy percent", and Yogesh was taking in the fuller picture.

qa.q: Why is Gargi's three-ways method fair?
qa.a: Saying the result as a gain, as a loss and in absolute numbers shows the full picture without pushing either school, so the family can choose clearly.

qa.q: How might the younger brother feel after Gargi's explanation?
qa.a: He may feel a little deflated that his exciting number lost its shine, but also clearer about what the brochures really say.

grounding: Shows a mature young adult restating a school choice as gain, as loss and in absolute numbers, framing it fairly rather than to steer the family.

passage: When I first became a project lead, I learned how easily I could steer people with words. I'm Ishita. We had to choose between two software vendors, and I preferred the cheaper one. My first draft of the email said, "Vendor A saves us 30%!" Then I remembered how I'd felt when Pranav once pitched something as "cuts risk by half" and I agreed without thinking. So I rewrote it: "Vendor A costs 30% less, about ₹4 lakh a year. It also has 20% more downtime, around three extra hours a month. Vendor B costs more and is steadier." Pranav read it and said, "I can't tell which one you like." That was the point. The team chose B, and I think they chose well.

qa.q: How much less does Vendor A cost per year?
qa.a: Vendor A costs 30% less, about ₹4 lakh a year.

qa.q: Why did Ishita remember Pranav's "cuts risk by half" pitch?
qa.a: Ishita felt uneasy remembering agreeing without thinking because of that wording, and didn't want to steer the team the same way.

qa.q: What made Ishita's rewritten email fair?
qa.a: It gave both the gain and the cost of each vendor in plain numbers, so the team could weigh them without being nudged by one shiny phrase.

qa.q: How might Pranav feel reading an email that hides Ishita's preference?
qa.a: Pranav may feel trusted to decide on the facts, and perhaps a little impressed that the email didn't try to sell anything.

grounding: Shows a young lead restating a choice as both gain and loss in absolute numbers and framing it fairly for others instead of steering them.

passage:
Supervisor's note, education NGO, Tuesday. Anand.
I watched Tarun, our youngest programme officer, speak to a room of parents about the new scholarship exam. The official poster says: "One in five students wins a scholarship!" Tarun didn't read it out. Instead he said, "Last year, 200 students took it. 40 won. 160 didn't. So it's worth trying, and it's also worth having a second plan." A few parents looked less excited, but more of them asked sensible questions: about fees if their child didn't win, about other schemes. One father told me afterwards it was the first time someone had given him the whole picture.
What I did: I asked Tarun to help us rewrite the poster the same way.

qa.q: How many students won the scholarship last year?
qa.a: Last year, 40 students won.

qa.q: Why did some parents look less excited after Tarun spoke?
qa.a: Hearing that 160 didn't win, not just "one in five", made the real odds clear, which dampened the excitement but helped them think.

qa.q: Why did Tarun's way of speaking lead to better questions?
qa.a: Giving the gain, the loss and the real numbers let parents plan for both outcomes, so they asked about fees and other schemes.

qa.q: How did the father who spoke to Anand experience Tarun's talk?
qa.a: He felt respected, saying it was the first time someone had given him the whole picture instead of a hopeful slogan. 🙏

grounding: Shows a young officer stating the scholarship odds as gain, loss and absolute numbers so parents can decide fairly rather than be steered.

passage:

qa.q: Why does Kishore decide Gurleen must have forgotten?

qa.q: What could Kishore think about the next time choosing a partner?
qa.a: Kishore could think about what the classmate has actually done, like finishing work or keeping promises, rather than how cheerful or tall they are.

qa.q: How might Miss feel on learning who really made the chart?
qa.a: Miss would probably feel sorry about praising the wrong child and want to give Kishore the credit.

grounding: Shows a child assuming a tall, cheerful classmate is also clever and honest, and explaining away her lie.

passage: In the village school near Ujjain, Manoj was the tallest boy in Class 5, always smiling, the first to be picked for kabaddi. Dhruv thought he must also be the smartest and the most honest. When Manoj said he'd return Dhruv's geometry box after the weekend, Dhruv handed it over without a thought. On Monday Manoj said he had lost it. On Wednesday Dhruv saw the same box, with his initials scratched inside, in Manoj's bag. His stomach twisted. But when he told his mother, he added quickly, "Maybe it's a different box. Manoj is good." She looked at him for a long moment.

qa.q: What did Dhruv see in Manoj's bag on Wednesday?
qa.a: He saw the same geometry box, with his initials scratched inside.

qa.q: Why does Dhruv say "Maybe it's a different box"?
qa.a: Manoj's height, smile and kabaddi skill made Dhruv believe he must be honest too, so the evidence feels wrong and gets explained away.

qa.q: How could Dhruv's mother help him?
qa.a: She could gently point to the initials, help him see that being cheerful or good at kabaddi says nothing about keeping promises, and help him ask for the box back.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's mother feel looking at him for a long moment?
qa.a: She may feel protective and a bit worried, seeing her son doubt his own eyes to keep believing in a classmate.

grounding: Shows a child assuming a tall, cheerful, popular classmate must be honest and explaining away clear evidence.

passage: On the first day of the new term in Lisbon, Paulo arrived: tall, sunburnt from summer, laughing at everything. By lunchtime Chidi had decided Paulo was the best at everything. "He'll be class captain," Chidi told his mother. "He's clever and he never lies, you can tell." In the pair maths quiz that afternoon, Chidi let Paulo decide every answer, even when Chidi thought differently. They got four out of ten. Two of the answers Chidi had wanted to write were right. "But Paulo looks so smart," Chidi said later, confused.

qa.a: They got four out of ten.

qa.q: Why did Chidi let Paulo decide every answer?
